title: Two same-named _AT Partials with the same static name build and pass
claim: Verdict: kept. One test holds `#include TEST_PARTIAL_PUBLIC_MODULE_AT(a, util)` and `#include TEST_PARTIAL_PUBLIC_MODULE_AT(b, util)`. Each `util.c` defines a static `util_helper` and a public function (`a_pub`, `b_pub`). The build compiles, links and passes (TESTED 1, PASSED 1). Ceedling writes `a/ceedling_partial_util_impl.{c,h}` and `b/ceedling_partial_util_impl.{c,h}` below `build/test/partials/test/test_collide/_t_/`. Their include guards differ (`GENB59956D4_A_CEEDLING_PARTIAL_UTIL_IMPL_H_CEEDLING` and `GEN7118F419_B_...`). PUBLIC mode leaves the static out of the generated source, so the shared static name never meets itself.

title: Same-named public or selected functions in two _AT modules fail at link
claim: Verdict: kept (inherent). Three variants fail with `multiple definition` at link, never at compile. (v2) both `util.c` define a public `util_pub`. (v1b) both public functions call `util_helper` and the test selects it with `TEST_PARTIAL_CONFIG_AT` for each module. (v3) both modules use `TEST_PARTIAL_PRIVATE_MODULE_AT`, which promotes the same-named statics. The fixture comment says the same. Directory qualification keeps the generated files apart but cannot keep the function names apart.

title: A variable name used by both same-named modules breaks compile or link
claim: Verdict: kept (inherent). When both `a/util.c` and `b/util.c` hold `static struct { int count; } s_ctx;`, the test fails to compile with `conflicting types for 'ceedling_partial_util_s_ctx_t'` and `conflicting types for 's_ctx'`. Both types headers (`a/` and `b/`) write `typedef struct { int count; } ceedling_partial_util_s_ctx_t;`. With a plain `static int s_count;` in both (no type) the build compiles and fails at link with `multiple definition`. With distinct variable names (`a_ctx`, `b_ctx`) it builds and passes. So the module-name-only type name collides only when the variable name also collides, and that variable collides without the type.

title: Mock Partials of same-named modules stay apart only through :mock_name_include_folder
claim: Verdict: kept (default on). `MOCK_PARTIAL_PUBLIC_MODULE_AT(a, util)` and `(b, util)` in one test build and pass. CMock names the lifecycle functions `a_Mockceedling_partial_util_interface_Init` and `b_...`, and the runner calls both. With `:cmock` ↳ `:mock_name_include_folder: FALSE` the same test fails at link with `multiple definition of Mockceedling_partial_util_interface_Init`, `_Verify` and `_Destroy`. The setting defaults to true in Ceedling and to false in CMock.

title: The module name in generated Partial type names carries no directory
claim: Verdict: kept. `Partials.type_name` folds `File.basename(module_name)`, so modules `a/util` and `b/util` both give `ceedling_partial_util_<variable>_t`. The experiment shows the same typedef name in both generated types headers. `PARTIAL_TYPE(util, s_ctx)` therefore cannot say which module it means.

title: A character a C identifier cannot hold becomes an underscore in Partial type names
claim: Verdict: kept. `CIdentifier.fold` replaces each `\W` character with `_`, one for one, and `Partials.type_name` applies it to the module's basename. `PARTIAL_TYPE` and `PARTIAL_LOCAL_TYPE` paste their arguments as tokens, so a test author writes the folded spelling (`my_sensor`), as the docs say.

title: A promoted function-scoped static is named from the function and variable, never the module
claim: Verdict: kept. The promoted name is `partial_<function>_<variable>` and carries no module part. File-scoped statics keep their own names and are declared `extern` in `_impl.h`. The docs promise uniqueness only among functions of one module. Two modules with a same-named function cannot be in one test in any case.

title: A Partial module name that is a predefined macro is replaced before it names the file
claim: Verdict: broken. In a GCC build the compiler predefines `unix` as 1. A test with `#include TEST_PARTIAL_PUBLIC_MODULE(unix)` and a `unix.c` module preprocesses to `#include "ceedling_partial_1_impl.h"`. Ceedling reads the directive as written and generates `ceedling_partial_unix_impl.{c,h}`. It also writes an empty `ceedling_partial_1_impl.h`. The test links without the module and fails with `undefined reference to 'unix_pub'`, under a notice that blames missing `#include` lines. `__PARTIALS_EXPAND(module)` expands the argument, and `_validate_module!` checks spelling only. This is the mechanism of #1460, which names the directory argument. The `_AT` module argument passes through `__PARTIALS_JOIN`, whose indirection also expands macros. That path was inferred and not built.

title: Generated Partial headers include their siblings by bare filename
claim: Verdict: kept, by the compiler's includer-directory rule. `a/ceedling_partial_util_impl.h` holds `#include "ceedling_partial_util_types.h"` and `a/ceedling_partial_util_impl.c` holds `#include "ceedling_partial_util_impl.h"`, with no directory. The test compile puts both `-I build/.../_t_/a` and `-I build/.../_t_/b` on the command line. Each bare include finds its own sibling only because GCC checks the includer's directory before the `-I` list. A resolver that skips the includer's directory would pick the first `-I` entry (`a/`) for `b/`'s include.

title: The runner of a test naming two same-named _AT Partials includes one impl header, by bare name
claim: Verdict: partly kept (observed, cause not traced). The test names `a/ceedling_partial_util_impl.h` and `b/ceedling_partial_util_impl.h`. Its generated runner holds one `#include "ceedling_partial_util_impl.h"` with no directory. The bare name resolves to `a/` by `-I` order. The test passes, since the runner needs neither header. I did not trace which step collapses the two includes. The runner spelling comes from `include.include_path || include.filename`.
